Question 1

Consider the portion of the surface z=sin⁡x+y whose projection onto the xy-plane is bounded by the curve y=4−x2, and the x-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.

a
∫−22∫04−x22+cos⁡xdydx
b
∫−22∫04−x21+sin⁡x+ydydx
c
∫−22∫04−x21+4cos2⁡xdydx
d
∫−22∫04−x22+cos2⁡xdydx
e
∫−22∫04−x21+sin2⁡x+y2dydx
Submit

decision.explanation: For z=f(x,y)=sin(x)+y, f_x=cos(x) and f_y=1. The surface-area element is sqrt(1+f_x²+f_y²) dy dx = sqrt(2+cos²(x)) dy dx. The projection is the upper semicircle: -2≤x≤2 and 0≤y≤sqrt(4-x²). Thus option d is correct.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Consider the portion of the surface $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by the curve $y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}},$ and the $x$-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y,\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071034/assets/8bf7a5921936b44a2e672fcee524c5a230800e6130f6c0a8683e6ce46829df58.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y)=1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

c

EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by z=f(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface area of S is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

z=sin⁡x+y,(x,y)∈D

where the region D is given by

D={(x,y):−2≤x≤2,0≤y≤4−x2},

as shown in the diagram below.

Now, since

∂z∂x=∂∂x(sin⁡x+y)=cos⁡x,∂z∂y=∂∂y(sin⁡x+y)=1,

the surface area is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬D1+(cos⁡x)2+(1)2dA=∬D2+cos2⁡xdA=∫−22∫04−x22+cos2⁡xdydx.

content.problem: Consider the portion of the surface $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by the curve $y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}},$ and the $x$-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y,\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071034/assets/8bf7a5921936b44a2e672fcee524c5a230800e6130f6c0a8683e6ce46829df58.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y)=1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Consider the portion of the surface z=yex whose projection onto the xy-plane is bounded by the lines y=2x, x=1, and the x-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.

a
∫01∫02x1+(y+1)exdydx
b
∫01∫02x1+y2exdydx
c
∫01∫02x1+(y+1)e2xdydx
d
∫01∫02x1+(y2+1)exdydx
e
∫01∫02x1+(y2+1)e2xdydx
Submit

decision.explanation: For z=ye^x, z_x=ye^x and z_y=e^x, so the surface-area integrand is sqrt(1+(ye^x)^2+(e^x)^2)=sqrt(1+(y²+1)e^(2x)). The triangular projection has bounds 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤2x. Therefore option e gives the required integral.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Consider the portion of the surface $z=y{e}^{x}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by the lines $y=2x,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=y{e}^{x},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2x},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071034/assets/903b7f3c6bd9721a974160487ca5099fdf54ce02b61697a7830bb662b26d8953.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{x})=y{e}^{x}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{x})={e}^{x},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(y{e}^{x})^{2}+({e}^{x})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+({y}^{2}+1){e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2x}\sqrt{1+({y}^{2}+1){e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={z}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,(y,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9,\,z\le 0},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071034/assets/cd5bcd7857769afb5f3a4f6197757c08eb295c7075a271c302c4b6087d661d14.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2z,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-2y)^{2}+(2z)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 3 \\ u & 1 & 37\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{37}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}{\int }_{1}^{37}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{37} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{37} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}[(37)^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{\pi (37\sqrt{37}-1)}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the hyperbolic paraboloid $x={z}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ that is subject to the constraints ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9$ and $z\le 0.$
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={z}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,(y,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9,\,z\le 0},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071034/assets/cd5bcd7857769afb5f3a4f6197757c08eb295c7075a271c302c4b6087d661d14.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2z,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-2y)^{2}+(2z)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 3 \\ u & 1 & 37\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{37}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}{\int }_{1}^{37}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{37} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{37} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}[(37)^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{\pi (37\sqrt{37}-1)}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $x=2-y-z$ that is subject to the constraints ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 1$ and $y\ge 0,\,z\ge 0.$
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x=2-y-z,\,(y,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 1,\,y\ge 0,\,z\ge 0},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071034/assets/3741c5db05232f04f60f747dc04176bfc77da30bbc39c79888cf4c18939369f7.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2-y-z)=-1, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2-y-z)=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+1+1}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{3}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot [\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $y=\frac{4}{7}{x}^{7/4}+z$ whose projection onto the $xz$-plane is bounded by $z=\sqrt{x},$ $x=4,$ and the $x$-axis.
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=\frac{4}{7}{x}^{7/4}+z,\,(x,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{x}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071034/assets/0a4ed826b683e7e8d8ed3e05bcb75618e74314febcdda8ae31b09f379ca21c73.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{4}{7}{x}^{7/4}+z)={x}^{3/4}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{4}{7}{x}^{7/4}+z)=1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{({x}^{3/4})}^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\cdot \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=2+{x}^{3/2},$ we get $\text{d}u=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 4 \\ u & 2 & 10\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\cdot \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{2}^{10}\frac{2}{3}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{2}^{10} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}({10}^{3/2}-{2}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{4}{9}(10\sqrt{10}-2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{9}(5\sqrt{5}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $y=\frac{4}{7}{x}^{7/4}+z$ whose projection onto the $xz$-plane is bounded by $z=\sqrt{x},$ $x=4,$ and the $x$-axis.
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=\frac{4}{7}{x}^{7/4}+z,\,(x,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{x}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071034/assets/0a4ed826b683e7e8d8ed3e05bcb75618e74314febcdda8ae31b09f379ca21c73.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{4}{7}{x}^{7/4}+z)={x}^{3/4}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{4}{7}{x}^{7/4}+z)=1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{({x}^{3/4})}^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\cdot \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=2+{x}^{3/2},$ we get $\text{d}u=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 4 \\ u & 2 & 10\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\cdot \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{2}^{10}\frac{2}{3}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{2}^{10} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}({10}^{3/2}-{2}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{4}{9}(10\sqrt{10}-2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{9}(5\sqrt{5}-1).\end{aligned}
$$
